title: Time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy with quantum light
abstract: We present a fully quantum theory of time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy, providing a general framework for describing the linear response of a nonequilibrium target to quantum probe fields beyond the semiclassical approximation. We elucidate how quantum correlations between probe-field frequency modes couple to coherences in the target and derive a simple expression for computing the resulting spectroscopic signals. We identify conditions under which quantum light can modify transient absorption spectra beyond the limits achievable with classical fields. Our work establishes a theoretical foundation for exploiting quantum light in ultrafast spectroscopy and suggests new routes for resolving dynamics in matter on timescales shorter than the duration of the probe pulse.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive quantum theory for Time-resolved Transient Absorption Spectroscopy, treating both the matter and the probe light quantum mechanically. It derives how quantum correlations within the probe field can alter the measured spectral signal beyond what classical light sources can achieve. This work provides a fundamental theoretical foundation for using quantum light in ultrafast spectroscopy.
main_problem: To develop a fully quantum theory for Time-resolved Transient Absorption Spectroscopy (TR-TAS) that accurately describes the linear response of a non-equilibrium target to quantum probe fields, moving beyond classical approximations.
main_result: The work establishes a general quantum framework showing that quantum correlations in the probe field can modify the transient absorption spectrum in ways unattainable with classical light sources.
method: The theory uses the von Neumann equation for the density matrix, quantizes the probe field using bosonic operators, and derives the measured signal by analyzing the expectation value of an effective photon-number operator.
model_or_system: The system involves a target (described by fermionic operators) coupled to a quantized electromagnetic probe field. The Hamiltonian includes terms for the target, the field, and their interaction, allowing for the calculation of field-matter correlations.
key_observables: The detected spectral intensity $I(\omega)$ or the effective photon-number operator $\hat{O}$, which is decomposed into background, interference, and radiation contributions.
important_parameters: The analysis considers various light states, including incoherent, coherent, and squeezed-light probes, and operates in the linear response regime.
main_assumptions: The initial state is assumed uncorrelated ($\hat{ho}(t_i) = \hat{ho}_t(t_i) \otimes \hat{ho}_b(t_i)$), and the theory builds upon the general quantum formulation of the interaction.
figures_summary: The notes detail the mathematical structure of the signal decomposition ($N_\omega = N_{	ext{bg},\omega} + N_{	ext{int},\omega} + N_{	ext{rad},\omega}$) and the derivation of field operator evolution in the Heisenberg picture.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general quantum framework, then decomposing the measured signal into distinct physical contributions (background, interference, radiation), and finally deriving the necessary field operator evolutions and correlation functions for specific light states like squeezed vacuum.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it pushes the theoretical description of ultrafast spectroscopy into the quantum regime, providing tools to predict and interpret signals generated by non-classical light sources.
